There is one behavior change when someone is using this `StringContent` constructor 
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/f6b6415119b4d6d4421b3186a6a8aaa4803af969/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/StringContent.cs#L56-L60
and passes `null` for `mediaType`. Or sets the `Headers.ContentType` to `null` after construction.
Then the browser wouldn't send a `Content-Type` anymore.

With the old logic the browser would send a `Content-Type` because of this browser behavior:
> When a string is used as a body, it conveniently sets the Content-Type header to text/plain;charset=UTF-8.

So with the new logic it would actually do what the developer wants and can also be seen as a bugfix.

---

Example:

```c#
new StringContent("Hello World", null, (System.Net.Http.Headers.MediaTypeHeaderValue)null);
```

Before (browser sets `Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8` because we send the body as `string`):
```
Accept: */*
Host: 127.0.0.1:36165
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/116.0.5845.0 Safari/537.36
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
Origin: http://127.0.0.1:39987
Referer: http://127.0.0.1:39987/
Content-Length: 11
sec-ch-ua: \"Chromium\";v=\"116\ \"Not)A;Brand\";v=\"24\ \"HeadlessChrome\";v=\"116\"
sec-ch-ua-platform: \"Linux\"
sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0
sec-fetch-site: cross-site
sec-fetch-mode: cors
sec-fetch-dest: empty
```

After (there is no `Content-Type` header):
```
Accept: */*
Host: 127.0.0.1:46361
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/116.0.5845.0 Safari/537.36
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Origin: http://127.0.0.1:43851
Referer: http://127.0.0.1:43851/
Content-Length: 11
sec-ch-ua: \"Chromium\";v=\"116\ \"Not)A;Brand\";v=\"24\ \"HeadlessChrome\";v=\"116\"
sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0
sec-ch-ua-platform: \"Linux\"
sec-fetch-site: cross-site
sec-fetch-mode: cors
sec-fetch-dest: empty
```

> So with the new logic it would actually do what the developer wants and can also be seen as a bugfix.

Sounds good.

Issue Details
While working on #91295 I noticed that there is a special handling for `StringContent`: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6d3be9e69dc385722851b0c165255cc4828aec7c/src/libraries/System.Net.Http/src/System/Net/Http/BrowserHttpHandler/BrowserHttpHandler.cs#L214-L227 But because `StringContent` inherits from `ByteArrayContent` the string is actually stored as a byte array, which means that `ReadAsStringAsync` actually allocates a new string an thus needs more memory than a call to `ReadAsByteArrayAsync` would need and is also slower. Since the browser supports sending byte array anyway I would propose to remove this special case. E.g. like this: https://github.com/campersau/runtime/commit/c887f0caf6b0329ef10272f1b8b0d4f41c7c5ec8 Or was there any other reason why this was special cased in the first place? | Method | Mean | Error | StdDev | Gen0 | Allocated | |--------------------- |---------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|----------:| | ReadAsStringAsync | 570.8 ns | 11.39 ns | 13.99 ns | 0.0973 | 1280 B | | ReadAsByteArrayAsync | 187.0 ns | 3.73 ns | 6.43 ns | 0.0525 | 688 B |
Benchmark ```c# [MemoryDiagnoser] public class Program { public static void Main(string[] args) { BenchmarkRunner.Run(args: args); } private StringContent content; [GlobalSetup] public void Setup() { content = new StringContent("Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, sed diam nonumy eirmod tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore magna aliquyam erat, sed diam voluptua. At vero eos et accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. Stet clita kasd gubergren, no sea takimata sanctus est Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consetetur sadipscing elitr, sed diam nonumy eirmod tempor invidunt ut labore et dolore magna aliquyam erat, sed diam voluptua. At vero eos et accusam et justo duo dolores et ea rebum. Stet clita kasd gubergren, no sea takimata sanctus est Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet."); } [Benchmark] public async Task ReadAsStringAsync() { await content.ReadAsStringAsync(); } [Benchmark] public async Task ReadAsByteArrayAsync() { await content.ReadAsByteArrayAsync(); } } ```
--- If we really want to remove allocations I would propose adding an `internal virtual bool TryGetMemory(out ReadOnlyMemory memory);` method to `HttpContent` and implement it for `ByteArrayContent` / `StringContent` / `EmptyContent` / `FormUrlEncodedContent` / `ReadOnlyMemoryContent` and special case this instead.

This also fixes a potential issue if someone passed `null` as `mediaType` to the `StringContent` constructor like this:
```c#
new StringContent("Hello World", null, (System.Net.Http.Headers.MediaTypeHeaderValue)null);
```
Or sets the `Headers.ContentType` to `null` after construction.

Because of this browser behavior:
> When a string is used as a body, it conveniently sets the Content-Type header to text/plain;charset=UTF-8.

a `Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8` is currently send.

But when sending a byte array there is no default browser behavior and the `Content-Type` would be correctly omitted.

See also https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/91463#issuecomment-1703034283 for more info.
